title: Finding Duplicates in an Array

phrases.explanation: Using more memory to reduce computation time, or vice versa. A fundamental concept in algorithm design.
A loop inside another loop. The inner loop runs completely for each iteration of the outer loop.
Processing each element in the array exactly once from start to end, achieving O(n) time.
Elements that are next to each other in the array. After sorting, duplicates become adjacent.
An operation that takes the same amount of time regardless of input size. Denoted as O(1).

technical_terms.definition: A collection that stores unique elements using a hash table. Lookup and insertion are O(1) on average.
Trying every possible combination. Often the simplest but least efficient approach.
How the running time grows relative to input size, expressed in Big-O notation.
How much additional memory an algorithm uses relative to input size.
An algorithm that uses only a constant amount of extra memory, O(1) space.

java_methods.description: Creates an empty hash set that stores unique integers.
Adds element to the set. Returns true if the element was not already present.
Returns true if the set already contains the element. O(1) average time.
Sorts the array in-place in ascending order. O(n log n) time.

concept: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice, and false if every element is distinct. The core question is: How can you efficiently detect if a duplicate exists?

solutions.label: Brute Force
solutions.summary: Compare every pair of elements using two nested loops.

solutions.label: Sorting
solutions.summary: Sort the array first, then check adjacent elements for duplicates.

solutions.label: Hash Set
solutions.summary: Use a hash set to track seen elements. If an element is already in the set, a duplicate exists.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph Array["nums = [1, 2, 3, 1]"]
        direction LR
        A0["1"] --- A1["2"] --- A2["3"] --- A3["1"]
    end
    Array --> Q{"Any duplicates?"}
    Q -->|"1 appears twice"| Yes["Return true"]
    style A0 fill:#f87171,stroke:#dc2626,color:#000
    style A3 fill:#f87171,stroke:#dc2626,color:#000
    style Yes fill:#4ade80,stroke:#16a34a,color:#000

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the problem I'd like you to solve. You're given an integer array. Your task is to determine whether any value in the array appears more than once. If any duplicate exists, return true. Otherwise, return false.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. Before I start, let me clarify a few things. What kind of integers are we dealing with? Can the array contain negative numbers?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, the array can contain any integers, including negative numbers. The array length can range from one to one hundred thousand elements.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. And what about edge cases? If the array has only one element, we should return false since there's nothing to compare against, right?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. A single-element array always returns false. An empty array also returns false.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Perfect. So to summarize, I need to check if any value repeats at least twice in the given integer array, handling arrays up to one hundred thousand elements efficiently. Let me walk through my thought process starting from the simplest approach.

sections.title: Level 1 — Brute Force
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph Input["nums = [3, 1, 3, 4]"]
        direction LR
        A0["3"] --- A1["1"] --- A2["3"] --- A3["4"]
    end
    Input --> Loop["Nested Loop: compare all pairs"]
    Loop --> C1["i=0, j=1: 3 ≠ 1"]
    Loop --> C2["i=0, j=2: 3 = 3 ✓"]
    C2 --> Result["Return true"]
    style C2 fill:#4ade80,stroke:#16a34a,color:#000
    style Result fill:#4ade80,stroke:#16a34a,color:#000

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Sounds good. What would the most straightforward solution look like?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The brute force approach would be to compare every pair of elements. For each element in the array, I check it against every other element that comes after it. If I find two elements that are equal, I return true. If I finish all pairs without a match, I return false. In code, that means two nested for-loops. The outer loop picks an element, and the inner loop scans the rest.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the time and space complexity of that approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The time complexity is O of n-squared, because we're checking roughly n times n-minus-one over two pairs. The space complexity is O of one since we're not using any extra data structures. This works, but it becomes extremely slow for large inputs. For an array of ten thousand elements, we could be making up to fifty million comparisons. So I'd like to optimize.

sections.title: Level 2 — Sorting Approach
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph Before["Before Sort"]
        direction LR
        B0["3"] --- B1["1"] --- B2["3"] --- B3["4"]
    end
    Before -->|"Arrays.sort()"| After
    subgraph After["After Sort"]
        direction LR
        S0["1"] --- S1["3"] --- S2["3"] --- S3["4"]
    end
    After --> Check["Compare adjacent pairs"]
    Check --> P1["1 ≠ 3"]
    Check --> P2["3 = 3 ✓"]
    P2 --> Result["Return true"]
    style S1 fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#000
    style S2 fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#000
    style P2 fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#000
    style Result fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#000

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good analysis. Can you do better than O of n-squared?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Yes. The key insight is that if we sort the array first, any duplicate elements will end up right next to each other. For example, if the input is three, one, three, four, two, after sorting it becomes one, two, three, three, four. Now the duplicate threes are adjacent.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: So the algorithm is: first, sort the array using a built-in sort like Arrays dot sort. Then iterate through the sorted array and compare each element with the next one. If any two adjacent elements are equal, return true. Otherwise, return false after the loop.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: And the complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The time complexity is O of n log n because the sorting step dominates. The space complexity is O of one additional space for most practical purposes. This is a big improvement. For ten thousand elements, instead of fifty million operations, we're doing roughly one hundred thirty thousand. But we can actually do even better.

sections.title: Level 3 — Hash Set (Optimal)
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph Input["nums = [1, 2, 3, 1]"]
        direction LR
        N0["1"] --- N1["2"] --- N2["3"] --- N3["1"]
    end
    Input --> Step1["Check 1 → not in set → add"]
    Step1 --> Set1["{1}"]
    Set1 --> Step2["Check 2 → not in set → add"]
    Step2 --> Set2["{1, 2}"]
    Set2 --> Step3["Check 3 → not in set → add"]
    Step3 --> Set3["{1, 2, 3}"]
    Set3 --> Step4["Check 1 → IN SET ✓"]
    Step4 --> Result["Return true"]
    style Step4 fill:#fb923c,stroke:#ea580c,color:#000
    style Result fill:#fb923c,stroke:#ea580c,color:#000

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the optimal approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: We can use a HashSet. A hash set lets us check whether an element already exists in O of one constant time on average. So instead of sorting or comparing every pair, we make a single pass through the array. For each element, we ask: have I seen this before? If yes, return true. If no, add it to the set and continue.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Can you walk me through an example?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Sure. Take the array one, two, three, one. We start with an empty hash set. We look at one. It's not in the set, so we add it. Now the set contains one. We look at two. Not in the set, add it. The set is one, two. We look at three. Not in the set, add it. The set is one, two, three. We look at one again, and this time it IS in the set. We return true immediately without checking the rest.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the complexity of this solution?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The time complexity is O of n because we visit each element exactly once, and each hash set operation is O of one on average. The space complexity is O of n because in the worst case, when there are no duplicates, the set stores all n elements. This is the classic time-space tradeoff. We use more memory to gain faster execution.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: How would you implement this in Java?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I'd create a new HashSet of Integer. Then loop through each number in the array. For each number, I call set dot contains to check if it's already there. If it returns true, I return true. Otherwise I call set dot add with that number. After the loop completes without finding a duplicate, I return false. Very clean and concise.

sections.diagram:
graph LR

        direction TB
        BF["Brute Force\nO(n²) time / O(1) space"] --> Sort["Sorting\nO(n log n) time / O(1) space"]
        Sort --> HS["Hash Set ★\nO(n) time / O(n) space"]
    end
    style BF fill:#60a5fa,stroke:#2563eb,color:#000
    style Sort fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#000
    style HS fill:#fb923c,stroke:#ea580c,color:#000

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great. Can you summarize all three approaches and their tradeoffs?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Of course. Level one, brute force: compare every pair using nested loops. O of n-squared time, O of one space. Level two, sorting: sort first then check adjacent elements. O of n log n time, O of one space. Level three, hash set: single pass with a set for O of one lookups. O of n time, O of n space. The hash set solution is optimal. We're trading O of n extra space for a huge improvement in time, from n-squared down to linear. This pattern of using a hash set for constant-time lookups shows up in many other problems, so it's a fundamental technique to master.
